projectedObliquity.source: Ahlers et al. (2020), AJ 160, 4 (arXiv:2004.14812), Table 2: lambda = -88 +/- 15 degrees from the gravity-darkened TESS transit. Gravity darkening alone cannot tell prograde from retrograde; the sign follows the Doppler tomography of Gaudi et al. (2017), lambda = -84.8 +/- 1.4 degrees, which the paper adopts for that choice (section 3.1).

stellarInclination.source: Ahlers et al. (2020), Table 2: i* = 52 +8/-7 degrees, defined in section 3.2 as 0 when the star is seen equator-on and 90 pole-on. In this record's convention, measured from the line of sight (90 equator-on), that is 90 - 52 = 38 degrees. Which pole is tilted toward us is not measured: 38 and 142 degrees fit alike, and the record uses the first.

trueObliquity.source: Ahlers et al. (2020), abstract and Table 2: psi = 87 +10/-11 degrees; the larger side is the tolerance.

equatorialRotationPeriod.source: Ahlers et al. (2020), Table 2: P* = 16 +5/-4 hours, from i* and v sin i = 111.4 +/- 1.3 km/s (Gaudi et al. 2017).

source: The star's spin axis measured against KELT-9b's orbit (Ahlers et al. 2020): the pole is built in the planet's sky frame from lambda and i*, with the orbit from packages/astronomy/data/bodies/kelt-9b.json, and the star turns once every 16 hours. The record's lambda, i* and the orbit's 86.79 degree inclination give psi 86.2 degrees, inside the published 87 +10/-11 degrees.
coordinateSystem: ICRF/J2000. +Z is the measured spin axis; +X faces the Sun at the scene epoch, so grid longitude 0 faces Earth; east longitude. The whole surface turns at one rate.
qualification: The orbit is nearly polar: KELT-9b passes over the star's poles. The axis's position angle on the sky is not measured; it is placed relative to the planet's orbit, whose orientation on the sky is a display convention (ascending node at position angle 0). Which of the two poles leans toward Earth is not measured (i* 38 or 142 degrees). The gravity-darkened surface is symmetric about the axis, so the turning is not visible.
